input:
Current use

The purpose of this section is to provide an overview of the current energy use at the paper mill, in order to establish a baseline against which potential improvements can be assessed. Electricity use at the mill currently stands at 2884 MWh per year. Of this total, refrigeration accounts for the largest share, representing the single biggest area of electricity consumption at the site. The remaining electricity is distributed across a wide range of drives and services, including stock preparation, refining, the paper machine drives, vacuum systems, compressed air, pumping, and lighting, as well as numerous smaller motors and items of auxiliary equipment. The electricity figures that are presented here are based on a full year of metering data, which means that the seasonal variations that occur within the year have already been taken into account in the totals. It is important to note that this assessment considers the mill in its current configuration, with its present product mix, machine schedule, and operating practices; any significant change in these areas would have an impact on both the overall electricity consumption and the way in which that consumption is distributed. Overall, the picture that emerges is one of a substantial electricity load that is heavily concentrated in refrigeration, which in turn suggests that measures targeting this area are likely to offer the most significant opportunities for improvement. It is also relevant to observe that the distribution of consumption is just as significant as the headline total itself. Where consumption is spread across a large number of small and disparate uses, it can be considerably more difficult to identify measures that are capable of delivering material savings, since no single intervention is able to address more than a small fraction of the total. In the present case, however, the concentration of consumption in one dominant area means that the assessment is able to focus its attention on the area where the greatest potential for improvement is understood to reside.

Refrigeration

Refrigeration represents the largest single use of electricity at the mill and therefore constitutes a key area of focus for this assessment. The refrigeration plant provides cooling for a number of important duties across the site, including chilled process water, cooling for air serving temperature-sensitive areas and equipment, and the removal of heat rejected by the process into its water circuits. Plant of this type typically operates for extended periods of time, with loads that vary in line with production, and the combined electricity consumption of its compressors, pumps, and heat-rejection equipment determines the overall cost of delivering the cooling duty. The efficiency with which the plant is operated and controlled has a direct bearing on the amount of electricity that a given duty requires; plant that runs at part load for extended periods, or that rejects heat at temperatures higher than necessary, will consume more electricity than the duty itself demands. Another important consideration is the heat that is rejected by the refrigeration plant at its condensers. This heat is currently discarded, but it has the potential to be recovered and put to use for heating duties elsewhere on the site, and it is this opportunity that the retrofit considered in the recommendation section seeks to exploit. A further point that deserves emphasis is that refrigeration plant of this kind is often operated for long periods at partial load, and the manner in which the plant responds to varying demand can have a substantial influence on the efficiency that is achieved in practice. Against this background, the opportunity to recover heat from the plant has attracted considerable interest, since it offers the prospect of deriving additional value from energy that is already being consumed by the site, rather than depending solely on reductions in the cooling duty itself.

Steam

Steam is used at the mill for a variety of heating duties, the most significant and continuous of which is the drying of the sheet on the paper machine. In addition to this, steam is used for process heating, space heating, and a range of smaller duties that are associated with production activities across the site. The steam figures that are available for the purposes of this assessment are drawn from one winter month. It should be borne in mind that a single winter month cannot be regarded as representative of the year as a whole, since steam demand is influenced by the heating season as well as by levels of production, and a winter month will tend to reflect the heating load at its highest. For this reason, no attempt has been made to annualise the steam figures, as doing so would risk presenting a misleading picture of the mill's annual steam consumption. The steam position is therefore reported here on the basis of one winter month only, and the scale of the annual steam load, together with any savings that might be available in this area, remains to be established once a full year of steam metering data has been collected. It is a common feature of assessments of this kind that the data available for different energy streams are not of equivalent quality or coverage, and the present assessment is no exception in this regard. Where the evidence base is incomplete, the appropriate response is to report the position transparently on the basis that is available, and to identify clearly the further information that would be required in order to place the relevant conclusions on a firmer footing.

Recommendation

It is recommended that the heat-recovery retrofit on the refrigeration plant be taken forward. The retrofit is projected to save 22% of electricity use, corresponding to a derived saving of 634 MWh per year when set against the current electricity use of 2884 MWh per year, at a capital cost of $396k. At an electricity price of $0.12 per kWh, the derived annual saving amounts to $76138, which gives a derived simple payback of 5.2 years. Site engineering will own the retrofit through the design and installation phases, and the savings that are achieved will be verified against metered electricity consumption following installation, using the same full-year basis as the current-use figures presented earlier in this assessment. In coming to this recommendation, account has been taken of the straightforward nature of the calculation that underlies the payback figure. The payback that is presented is a simple payback, and it does not seek to incorporate factors such as the time value of money, future movements in electricity prices, or the maintenance requirements of the new equipment. It is considered, however, that this level of analysis is entirely appropriate for the purpose of screening the proposal at this stage, and that the figures provide a sound basis on which the decision can be taken. It should be emphasised that this recommendation relates to the electricity side of the mill's energy use only. The steam figures underpinning this assessment are derived from one winter month and are accordingly flagged as seasonal in nature; no steam-side measure is therefore recommended at this stage, and it is suggested that a full year of steam metering be obtained before any steam-side proposal is developed, in order to ensure that any such measure is appropriately sized against demand across the whole year rather than against a single, unrepresentative month.
target:
Current use

Electricity use at the mill is 2884 MWh per year. Refrigeration takes the largest share of that use. The remainder is spread across the mill's drives and services: stock preparation, refining, the paper machine drives, vacuum systems, compressed air, pumping, and lighting, together with the smaller motors and auxiliaries that serve them. The electricity figures rest on a full year of metering, so the seasonal movement of load inside the year is already averaged into the total. The assessment takes the mill as it currently runs, at its present product mix, machine schedule, and operating practice; a change to any of those moves both the electricity total and the shares within it. What the current-use picture establishes is the scale of the electricity load and where the load sits. The total is large enough that a saving measured as a share of it is a large saving in absolute terms, and the concentration of use in refrigeration is what makes a single retrofit measure worth assessing in detail, rather than a programme of small measures spread thinly across many small loads. Steam is raised and used alongside electricity at the mill, and the steam position is treated in its own section below, on the basis stated there. The shares within the total matter as much as the total itself. A load spread evenly across many small uses leaves no single point of attack, whereas a load concentrated in one large use can be addressed by one measure, assessed once, with its saving read off the site meters. The mill load has the second shape. It also has a shape in time: production loads follow the machine schedule while service loads follow occupancy and season, and the year of metering contains both. Ranking the uses needs the total and the shares, and both stand on the year of metering, so the ranking does not wait on separating those shapes.

Refrigeration

Refrigeration is the largest single use of electricity at the mill. The refrigeration plant serves the cooling duties the process depends on: chilled process water, cooling for air that serves temperature-sensitive areas and equipment, and the removal of heat that the process itself rejects into its water circuits. Refrigeration plant of this kind runs for long hours at loads that follow production, and its compressors, pumps, and heat-rejection equipment together set the electricity the duty costs. The efficiency of the plant as installed and as controlled decides how much electricity a given cooling duty takes; a plant that runs at part load for much of its time, or that rejects its heat at a higher temperature than the sink requires, spends electricity that the duty itself does not demand. The heat the refrigeration plant rejects is the point of contact with the rest of the mill's energy system. Rejected heat leaves the plant at the condenser, and heat recovered there can serve heating duties elsewhere on site that are currently met from other energy. That recovery is the retrofit assessed in the recommendation: it acts on the largest load on the site, and it acts on heat the site already produces and currently throws away. Two features of the plant decide how much of the rejected heat a retrofit can use. The first is temperature: heat rejected above the temperature a receiving duty needs can pass into that duty directly, while heat rejected below it cannot serve without being upgraded. The second is timing: recovery serves a heating duty only when the refrigeration plant is rejecting heat at the hours the duty calls for it. A recovery scheme is therefore matched, duty by duty, against the site heating loads, and the match, not the raw quantity of rejected heat, sets the saving the scheme can deliver.

Steam

Steam serves the mill's heating duties, of which the drying of the sheet on the paper machine is the largest and the most continuous. Steam also serves process heating, space heating, and the smaller duties that follow production around the site. The steam figures available to this assessment are from one winter month. A single winter month does not stand for the year: steam demand follows the heating season as well as production, and a winter month carries the heating load at its heaviest while the rest of the year runs lighter. No annual steam figure is stated in this assessment, because annualising the winter month would build the year's steam position on the least representative month available. The steam side of the mill's energy use is therefore recorded here as a position in one winter month only, and the size of the annual steam load, and of any saving available against it, stays open until steam metering covers a full year. The position would be different if the winter month stood as one month among twelve. On its own it fixes the scale of steam use in the heaviest month and nothing more: it cannot show how far demand falls in the lighter months, how steam use tracks production across the year, or what a steam-side measure would save in a full year. Those are the quantities a steam-side proposal would need, and they are the reason the steam side of this assessment is left as a stated limit rather than built into figures the evidence does not support.

Recommendation

The heat-recovery retrofit on the refrigeration plant is recommended. The retrofit is projected to save 22% of electricity use, a derived saving of 634 MWh per year against the current use of 2884 MWh per year, at a capital cost of $396k. At $0.12 per kWh, the derived annual saving is $76138, and the derived simple payback is 5.2 years. Site engineering owns the retrofit through design and installation, and the saving is to be verified against metered electricity use after installation, on the same full-year basis as the current-use figures. The payback is a simple payback: it divides the capital cost by the annual saving and takes no account of the timing of cash flows within the period, of maintenance on the retrofit, or of movement in the electricity price after installation. It is stated as derived because each of its inputs is stated: the saving share, the current use, the price, and the capital cost. If the electricity price moves, the annual saving moves with it and the payback moves inversely; the saving in energy, which the retrofit physically delivers, does not move. The recommendation therefore rests on the energy saving first and on the money saving at the stated price second. The recommendation is made on the electricity side only. The steam figures behind this assessment are from one winter month and are flagged as seasonal; no steam-side measure is recommended on that basis, and a full year of steam metering should precede any steam-side proposal, so that a steam measure is sized against the year's demand and not against its heaviest month.
